stem: The student wants to present the aim of Ramanathan's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Downbursts are powerful downward gusts of air from thunderstorms that can flatten crops and endanger aircraft.
• Many downbursts are too small or too brief for conventional radar networks to detect.
• In 2023, atmospheric scientist Priya Ramanathan led a team that investigated whether low-cost wind sensors mounted on farm irrigation towers could detect downbursts.
• The team installed 140 sensors across 60 square kilometers of Nebraska farmland.
• Over one summer, the sensors recorded 23 downbursts that radar had missed.
choices: Many downbursts, gusts that can flatten crops and endanger aircraft, are too small or too brief for conventional radar to detect.
Ramanathan's team set out to determine whether inexpensive wind sensors on irrigation towers could detect downbursts.
Ramanathan's team set out to show that sensors on irrigation towers could replace radar networks for tracking thunderstorms.
Ramanathan's team found that wind sensors on irrigation towers recorded 23 downbursts that radar had missed.
explanation: The goal asks for the aim, meaning the question the study set out to answer. The notes state that aim directly: the team investigated whether low-cost sensors on irrigation towers could detect downbursts. Choice B restates that question with the words 'set out to determine whether,' which is the language of an aim, and it adds nothing the notes don't support.

A.why: You picked the background. This sentence explains why the study mattered, but it never mentions Ramanathan's study or what the study wanted to find out.

C.why: It's phrased like an aim, but it misstates the aim. The team asked whether sensors could detect downbursts. The notes never say the team wanted to replace radar or track thunderstorms in general.

D.why: This is the study's result, not its aim. You matched the goal to the wrong stage of the research: 'found' reports what happened, not what the team set out to learn.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion of Wierzbicki's research. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Plant leaves have stomata, tiny pores through which the plant takes in carbon dioxide.
• Plants tend to grow fewer stomata when atmospheric carbon dioxide levels are high.
• Paleobotanist Tomasz Wierzbicki counted stomata on fossil ginkgo leaves from 56-million-year-old rock layers in Greenland.
• The fossil leaves had about 40 percent fewer stomata per square millimeter than modern ginkgo leaves.
• Wierzbicki concluded that carbon dioxide levels 56 million years ago were substantially higher than they are today.
choices: Fossil ginkgo leaves from Greenland had about 40 percent fewer stomata per square millimeter than modern ginkgo leaves have.
Wierzbicki counted the stomata on fossil ginkgo leaves preserved in 56-million-year-old rock layers in Greenland.
Wierzbicki concluded that ginkgo trees grew fewer stomata 56 million years ago because Greenland's climate was warmer.
Wierzbicki concluded that atmospheric carbon dioxide was substantially higher 56 million years ago than it is today.
explanation: A conclusion is what the researcher decided the evidence means. The stomata count is the evidence. Wierzbicki's conclusion is about carbon dioxide levels in the past, and Choice D states exactly that, just as the last note records it.

A.why: This is the finding, the raw result of the count, not the conclusion drawn from it. The subtlety at this level is that 'finding' and 'conclusion' are separate stages. The goal asks for what the result means, which is higher carbon dioxide.

B.why: This describes the method: what Wierzbicki did. It doesn't say what he found or what he concluded.

C.why: It uses the word 'concluded' but attributes a conclusion the notes never state. According to the notes, fewer stomata point to high carbon dioxide, not a warmer climate. This choice replaces the real cause with a different one.

stem: The student wants to present Okafor's study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Heat waves raise the risk of hospitalization for older adults who live alone.
• In 2022, the city of Marlow Falls began a program in which volunteers phone residents over 70 on days above 35°C.
• Epidemiologist Ines Okafor compared heat-related hospitalizations among 3,000 program participants and 3,000 similar nonparticipants over two summers.
• Participants were hospitalized for heat-related illness 31 percent less often than nonparticipants.
choices: Comparing 3,000 phone-call program participants with 3,000 similar nonparticipants, Okafor found that participants had 31 percent fewer heat-related hospitalizations.
Over two summers, Okafor compared heat-related hospitalizations among 3,000 participants in a phone-call program and 3,000 similar nonparticipants.
Residents in Marlow Falls' phone-call program were hospitalized for heat-related illness 31 percent less often than residents who did not take part.
Okafor's study showed that phoning older residents on hot days prevents 31 percent of all heat-related hospitalizations in Marlow Falls.
explanation: The goal has two parts: the study and its findings. Choice A covers both. It names the study (Okafor's comparison of 3,000 participants with 3,000 nonparticipants) and its result (31 percent fewer heat-related hospitalizations), and it connects them with 'found that.'

B.why: This is only half the goal. It describes the study's design but never says what the study found.

C.why: This is the other half. It gives the result but doesn't mention Okafor or her comparison, so the reader never learns about the study that produced it.

D.why: The study compared two groups of 3,000 people. It didn't measure 'all heat-related hospitalizations in Marlow Falls,' so this choice stretches a result about one sample to the whole city.

stem: The student wants to present the aim of Marchetti and Asante's research. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Indigo was the most widely used blue dye in eighteenth-century European textiles.
• Historians had long assumed that the indigo in eighteenth-century French fabrics came mainly from Caribbean plantations.
• Conservation scientists Hélène Marchetti and Kofi Asante wanted to know whether some of that indigo came instead from woad, a plant grown in France.
• They analyzed chemical impurities in dye samples from 85 surviving French garments.
• Impurities typical of woad appeared in 38 of the samples.
choices: Historians had long assumed that the indigo in eighteenth-century French fabrics came mainly from plantations in the Caribbean.
Marchetti and Asante detected impurities typical of woad in 38 of 85 dye samples from eighteenth-century French garments.
Marchetti and Asante sought to learn whether some indigo in eighteenth-century French fabrics came from woad, a French-grown plant.
Marchetti and Asante sought to confirm that the indigo in eighteenth-century French fabrics came from Caribbean plantations.
explanation: An aim is the question the researchers wanted to answer. The third note says Marchetti and Asante wanted to know whether some of the indigo came from woad. Choice C restates that question using 'sought to learn whether.'

A.why: This is the background assumption the researchers questioned. It gives the reason the study was needed, not what the researchers set out to learn.

B.why: This is the result. 'Detected' reports what the analysis found, which is a later stage of the research than the aim.

D.why: It sounds like an aim, but it reverses the real one. The researchers were testing the Caribbean assumption by asking about woad, not trying to confirm it. When two choices both start with 'sought to,' check which one matches the note.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion that Reyes-Moreau's team reached. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hot Jupiters are giant planets that orbit extremely close to their stars.
• One hypothesis holds that they formed farther out and migrated inward violently, scattering any smaller planets in their path.
• Astronomer Daniel Reyes-Moreau's team searched 60 hot-Jupiter systems for additional planets.
• The team detected small companion planets near the hot Jupiter in 11 of those systems.
• The team concluded that at least some hot Jupiters formed in place or migrated inward gently.
choices: One hypothesis holds that hot Jupiters formed farther from their stars and scattered smaller planets as they migrated inward.
Reyes-Moreau's team concluded that at least some hot Jupiters formed where they are now or migrated inward gently.
Reyes-Moreau's team detected small companion planets near the hot Jupiter in 11 of the 60 systems it searched.
Reyes-Moreau's team concluded that no hot Jupiter could have formed farther out and migrated inward violently.
explanation: The goal asks for the conclusion, which the last note gives: at least some hot Jupiters formed in place or migrated gently. Choice B states it and keeps the qualifier 'at least some,' and that qualifier is what separates it from the overreaching choice.

A.why: This is the background hypothesis the study tested. It describes a debate, not what the team concluded.

C.why: This is the finding, the observation the conclusion rests on. The goal asks what the team decided the observation means.

D.why: It drops the qualifier. Finding companions in 11 of 60 systems supports a claim about 'at least some' hot Jupiters, not a claim that rules out violent migration for every one of them.

stem: The student wants to present the recommendation that resulted from Lindqvist's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Many distance runners stretch statically, holding each stretch for 30 seconds or more, before races.
• Sports scientist Maren Lindqvist tested how pre-run static stretching affects performance.
• Forty-eight trained runners completed 3-kilometer time trials after either static stretching or a dynamic warm-up of leg swings and skips.
• Times after static stretching averaged 2.1 percent slower.
• Lindqvist advises runners to replace pre-race static stretching with a dynamic warm-up.
choices: Lindqvist advises runners to swap the static stretching they do before races for a dynamic warm-up of leg swings and skips.
In Lindqvist's study, 3-kilometer times averaged 2.1 percent slower after static stretching than after a dynamic warm-up.
Lindqvist had 48 trained runners complete 3-kilometer time trials after either static stretching or a dynamic warm-up.
Lindqvist advises runners to avoid all stretching before races, since stretching made runners 2.1 percent slower.
explanation: A recommendation is advice, so look for the choice that tells runners what to do. Choice A gives Lindqvist's advice as the notes state it: replace static stretching with a dynamic warm-up before races.

B.why: This is the result that led to the advice, not the advice. It tells you what happened in the trials, not what runners should do.

C.why: This is the method. It describes how the study worked and contains no recommendation.

D.why: It's phrased as advice, but it goes further than Lindqvist does. Her recommendation keeps a dynamic warm-up, and only static stretching was linked to slower times. 'Avoid all stretching' isn't supported.

stem: The student wants to describe the method Haddad used in her study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tel Varesh is the site of an ancient hilltop settlement.
• Archaeologists have debated whether the settlement was occupied year-round or only seasonally.
• Archaeologist Nadia Haddad examined 900 goat teeth recovered from the site's refuse pits.
• She measured growth layers in the teeth's enamel, which record the season in which an animal died.
• The teeth showed deaths in every season, suggesting that people lived at Tel Varesh year-round.
choices: Archaeologists have debated whether the hilltop settlement at Tel Varesh was occupied year-round or only seasonally.
Haddad's analysis of goat teeth suggested that the hilltop settlement at Tel Varesh was occupied year-round.
Haddad counted the goat teeth in Tel Varesh's refuse pits to estimate how many people had lived at the settlement.
Haddad measured enamel growth layers, which record season of death, in 900 goat teeth from the site's refuse pits.
explanation: A method is what the researcher actually did. According to the notes, Haddad measured enamel growth layers in 900 goat teeth, and those layers show when each animal died. Choice D describes that procedure and explains why it is useful.

A.why: This is the background debate. It explains why the question mattered but says nothing about how Haddad studied it.

B.why: This is the study's conclusion. It names the goat teeth in passing but reports what the analysis suggested, not how the analysis was done.

C.why: It describes a method, but not Haddad's. She measured growth layers to find out the season of death. According to the notes, she didn't count teeth to estimate population.

stem: The student wants to present Varma's study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Artificial light at night can disrupt the behavior of nocturnal insects.
• Ecologist Sunita Varma wanted to know whether streetlights affect how often moths visit night-blooming flowers.
• Her team compared 20 meadow plots lit by LED streetlights with 20 unlit plots.
• Flowers in the lit plots received 58 percent fewer moth visits than flowers in the unlit plots.
choices: Varma's team compared moth visits to night-blooming flowers in 20 meadow plots lit by LED streetlights and in 20 unlit plots.
Varma set out to learn whether streetlights affect how often moths visit the flowers of night-blooming plants in meadows.
Comparing lit and unlit meadow plots, Varma's team found that flowers under LED streetlights got 58 percent fewer moth visits.
Varma's study found that LED streetlights reduce the pollination of all night-blooming plants by about 58 percent.
explanation: The goal asks for the study and its findings, so the answer has to name the study and its result together. Choice C does both. It identifies the comparison between lit and unlit plots, then reports the finding of 58 percent fewer moth visits, joined by 'found that.'

A.why: This covers only the study. It describes the comparison thoroughly but never gives the result.

B.why: This is the aim. It tells you what Varma wanted to learn, but not how she studied it or what she found.

D.why: The study measured moth visits in 40 meadow plots. It didn't measure pollination, and it didn't cover all night-blooming plants. This choice claims more than the data show.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the aim of Okonkwo's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lake-effect snow forms when cold air moves across a lake whose water is warmer than the air.
• The snow often falls in narrow bands, and forecasters have long struggled to predict exactly where those bands will land.
• In 2023, atmospheric scientist Rhea Okonkwo and her team investigated whether drone readings of air temperature just above a lake's surface could improve forecasts of where snow bands would fall.
• The team flew drones over Lake Erie during 14 winter storms.
• Forecasts that used the drone data placed snow bands within 5 km of their actual location 78% of the time, compared with 52% for standard forecasts.
choices: Across 14 storms over Lake Erie, forecasts that used drone data placed snow bands within 5 km of their actual location 78% of the time.
Okonkwo's team investigated whether drone readings of air temperature just above Lake Erie could help forecasters pinpoint where snow bands would fall.
Okonkwo's team set out to show that drones could fully replace standard forecasts for predicting lake-effect snowfall across the Great Lakes.
Because lake-effect snow falls in narrow bands, forecasters have long struggled to predict exactly where that snow will land.
explanation: The goal asks for the aim, which is the question the study set out to answer. Choice B is built around that stage. It uses 'investigated whether' and states the question itself: could drone temperature readings help forecasters pinpoint where snow bands would fall? That matches the third note.

A.why: You picked the study's result instead of its aim. This is the trap for this subtype: the choice reports what the team found, the 78% figure, but the goal asked what the team was trying to find out.

C.why: You were drawn by 'set out to,' which sounds like an aim, but the aim stated here goes beyond the notes. The team asked whether drones could improve forecasts. It did not try to show that drones could replace standard forecasts, and it did not study all of the Great Lakes.

D.why: You chose the background, meaning the problem that came before the study. This sentence never mentions Okonkwo's team or what they set out to learn, so it can't present the study's aim.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion Ibarra drew from his study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Several US cities have passed "fair workweek" laws requiring retail employers to post shift schedules at least two weeks in advance.
• Critics argued that such laws would lead employers to cut workers' hours.
• From 2019 to 2022, economist Tomás Ibarra tracked 1,200 retail workers, some in cities with fair workweek laws and some in cities without them.
• Weekly hours did not differ significantly between the two groups, but workers covered by the laws reported 30% fewer last-minute shift cancellations.
• Ibarra concluded that the laws made schedules more predictable without reducing workers' hours.
choices: From 2019 to 2022, Ibarra tracked 1,200 retail workers, some in cities with fair workweek laws and some in cities without them.
Critics of fair workweek laws argued that requiring schedules two weeks in advance would lead employers to cut workers' hours.
Ibarra concluded that fair workweek laws made retail schedules more predictable but also led employers to reduce workers' hours.
Ibarra concluded that fair workweek laws made retail schedules more predictable without reducing the hours that workers received.
explanation: The goal names the conclusion stage, so you need the choice that reports what Ibarra concluded and reports it accurately. Choice D matches the last note on both points: the laws made schedules more predictable, and they did not cut hours.

A.why: You picked the method instead of the conclusion. This is the trap for this subtype: the choice tells how Ibarra ran the study (who he tracked and when), but not what he concluded.

B.why: You chose the background debate. This is the critics' prediction from before the study, not Ibarra's conclusion. In fact, his findings went against it.

C.why: You matched the wording 'Ibarra concluded,' but you missed the second half. The notes say hours did not differ significantly and that Ibarra found no reduction in hours. This choice says the opposite.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the aim of Ferrer's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Slow slip events are episodes in which a fault moves gradually over days or weeks without producing strong shaking.
- In 2024, seismologist Lucía Ferrer and her colleagues placed seafloor pressure sensors along a subduction zone off southern Chile.
- The team wanted to determine whether slow slip events tend to occur before larger earthquakes on the same fault.
- Over three years, the sensors recorded eleven slow slip events.
- Four of the eleven events were followed within a month by an earthquake of magnitude 5 or greater.
choices: Ferrer's team set out to learn whether slow slip events, in which a fault moves gradually, tend to come before larger earthquakes on the same fault.
Of the eleven slow slip events that Ferrer's team recorded, four were followed within a month by an earthquake of magnitude 5 or greater.
Ferrer's team placed seafloor pressure sensors along a subduction zone off southern Chile and recorded data there for three years.
Ferrer's team showed that slow slip events, in which a fault moves gradually, cause the larger earthquakes that later strike the same fault.
explanation: The goal asks for the study's aim, meaning what the researchers were trying to find out. Choice A states that aim directly with 'set out to learn whether', which matches the note about what the team wanted to determine. It also adds a brief definition of slow slip events.

B.why: You picked the study's result. Four out of eleven events is what the team found, not what they were trying to find out. The goal asked for the aim.

C.why: You picked the method. Placing sensors and recording for three years describes how the team did the study, not what question it was meant to answer.

D.why: This choice turns the study into a proven claim that slow slip events cause larger earthquakes. The notes never say that. Only four of eleven events were followed by a larger quake, and the team only asked whether the events tend to come first. The choice also reports a conclusion instead of an aim.

stem: The student wants to present Wrona's study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Musicologists have long debated whether Baroque violinists used vibrato continuously or only as an occasional ornament.
- Musicologist Tomasz Wrona examined 214 surviving violin parts copied between 1690 and 1750.
- He counted how often a wavy-line symbol, which indicated vibrato, appeared above sustained notes.
- The symbol appeared above fewer than 6 percent of sustained notes.
- Wrona concluded that Baroque violinists likely used vibrato sparingly, as an ornament.
choices: In a study of 214 violin parts copied between 1690 and 1750, Wrona found that a vibrato symbol appeared above fewer than 6 percent of sustained notes.
Wrona examined 214 violin parts copied between 1690 and 1750, counting how often a wavy-line symbol indicating vibrato appeared above sustained notes.
Musicologists have long debated whether Baroque violinists used vibrato continuously or used it only as an occasional ornament in their playing.
In a study of 214 violin parts copied between 1690 and 1750, Wrona found that a vibrato symbol appeared above most of the sustained notes.
explanation: The goal asks for two things: the study and its findings. Choice A names the study (214 violin parts from 1690 to 1750) and gives the result the notes report, fewer than 6 percent of sustained notes. It is the only choice that includes both parts accurately.

B.why: This choice describes the study and its method but never says what Wrona found. The goal asked for the study and its findings, so half the job is missing.

C.why: You picked the background debate that led to the study. It mentions neither Wrona's study nor its result.

D.why: This choice has the right structure, a study plus a finding, but it gets the finding backward. The notes say the symbol appeared above fewer than 6 percent of sustained notes, not most of them.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion that Osei's team reached. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In many bird species, individuals living in noisy cities sing at higher pitches than rural members of the same species.
- Ornithologist Amara Osei and her team asked whether this shift in song sparrows is learned or inherited.
- They hand-raised song sparrow chicks from city nests and rural nests together in the same quiet aviary.
- As adults, the birds from city nests sang at about the same pitch as the birds from rural nests.
- The team concluded that city song sparrows learn their higher pitch from their surroundings rather than inheriting it.
choices: Osei's team investigated whether city song sparrows' higher-pitched songs are learned from their surroundings or inherited from their parents.
Osei's team hand-raised song sparrow chicks from city nests and from rural nests together in the same quiet aviary until adulthood.
Osei's team concluded that city song sparrows learn their higher-pitched songs from their surroundings rather than inheriting them.
Osei's team concluded that city song sparrows inherit their higher-pitched songs from their parents rather than learning them.
explanation: The goal asks for the conclusion. Choice C uses 'concluded' and states what the team decided: the higher pitch is learned from surroundings, not inherited. That matches the last note exactly.

A.why: You picked the study's aim. 'Investigated whether... or...' states the question the team asked, not the answer it reached. Both options are still open in this sentence, so it gives no conclusion.

B.why: You picked the method. Raising the chicks together in a quiet aviary is how the team tested the question, not what it concluded.

D.why: This choice reverses the conclusion. City-hatched birds raised in quiet conditions sang like rural birds, so the team concluded the pitch is learned, not inherited.

stem: The student wants to present the aim of Okafor's study. Which choice does NOT effectively use relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sprinters often hold static stretches as part of their warm-up before races.
• Some coaches worry that static stretching briefly reduces muscle power.
• In 2024, sports scientist Lena Okafor investigated whether a 90-second static calf stretch affects 30-meter sprint times.
• She timed 24 collegiate sprinters once after stretching and once after no stretching.
• The times differed by less than 0.02 seconds, a gap she judged too small to matter in competition.
choices: Okafor's 2024 study sought to determine whether a 90-second static calf stretch affects sprinters' 30-meter times.
Does a 90-second static calf stretch change how fast sprinters run 30 meters? Okafor set out to answer that question.
Responding to coaches' concerns, Okafor investigated whether a 90-second static calf stretch alters 30-meter sprint times.
Okafor found that a 90-second static calf stretch changed collegiate sprinters' 30-meter times by less than 0.02 seconds.
explanation: The goal names one stage of the study: its aim, meaning the question Okafor set out to answer. Choice D reports what she found (a difference of less than 0.02 seconds), which is the result, not the purpose. Every word of it is accurate, but it describes the wrong stage, so it is the one choice that fails the goal. A, B, and C all state what Okafor was trying to learn.

A.why: You may have thought 'sought to determine' claims more than the notes support. It doesn't. It just restates 'investigated whether,' which is the aim. This choice accomplishes the goal.

B.why: You may have rejected this because it opens with a question rather than a statement. Asking the question the study was built to answer and then saying Okafor 'set out to answer' it is a direct way to present the aim. Judge the content, not the form.

C.why: You probably saw the background note about coaches and decided this describes the wrong stage. That background is only an opening phrase. The main clause, 'Okafor investigated whether…,' is the aim, so this choice does the job.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion of Mehta's study. Which choice does NOT effectively use relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Forecasters predict fog mainly from models of air temperature and humidity.
• Dense fog near airports can ground or delay flights.
• In 2025, meteorologist Arjun Mehta tested whether soil moisture readings improve fog forecasts at an inland airport.
• He compared forecasts made with and without soil data over 120 nights.
• Forecasts using soil data correctly predicted fog on 18 more nights.
• Mehta concluded that fog models for inland airports should include soil moisture readings.
choices: Mehta concluded that the fog models used to forecast conditions at inland airports should include soil moisture readings.
According to Mehta, soil moisture readings belong in the models that forecasters use to predict fog at inland airports.
Mehta compared fog forecasts made with and without soil moisture readings at an inland airport over 120 nights.
Because soil data caught fog on 18 more nights, Mehta concluded that inland airport fog models should use it.
explanation: The goal asks for Mehta's conclusion, which is the point he drew at the end: inland airport fog models should include soil moisture readings. Choice C accurately describes his method (comparing forecasts over 120 nights) but never says what he concluded. It presents the wrong stage of the study, so it is the one that fails. A, B, and D all state the conclusion.

A.why: You may have thought this reads more like a recommendation than a conclusion. In these notes, Mehta's conclusion is that recommendation, and this choice states it directly with 'concluded that.' It accomplishes the goal.

B.why: You may have thought 'belong in the models' goes further than the notes. It is a restatement of 'should include soil moisture readings,' credited to Mehta, so it presents his conclusion faithfully.

D.why: You probably saw the result about 18 more nights and decided this was the wrong stage. The result is only the supporting 'because' clause. The main clause, 'Mehta concluded that…,' presents the conclusion, so this choice does what the goal asks.

stem: The student wants to present the study's finding about the difference between the two kinds of slabs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Road salt can seep into concrete bridge decks and corrode the steel bars inside them.
• Civil engineer Adaeze Okafor and her team tested whether bars made of basalt fiber resist salt damage longer than steel bars.
• Over 18 months, they sprayed 24 concrete test slabs, some with each kind of bar, with salt water again and again.
• On average, steel-reinforced slabs cracked after 210 cycles, while basalt-reinforced slabs cracked after 540.
• The team concluded that basalt bars could help bridge decks last longer in cold climates.
choices: Okafor's team set out to learn whether basalt-fiber bars would hold up against salt damage longer than the steel bars found in most bridge decks.
Over 18 months, Okafor's team repeatedly sprayed 24 concrete test slabs, some reinforced with steel and some with basalt fiber, with salt water.
Basalt-reinforced slabs lasted an average of 540 salt-spray cycles before cracking, more than twice as many as the 210 cycles steel-reinforced slabs lasted.
Okafor's team showed that basalt-fiber bars will make every bridge deck in a cold climate last more than twice as long as a deck with steel bars.
explanation: The goal asks for the finding about the difference between the two kinds of slabs, so the right choice has to give the result for both kinds and show how far apart they were. Choice C gives both averages (540 and 210 cycles) and names the gap: basalt slabs lasted more than twice as many cycles.

A.why: You picked the study's aim. This sentence says what the team wanted to find out, but it never says what they found, so the difference between the slabs is missing.

B.why: You picked the method. It describes how the slabs were tested, but it gives no result, so the student's reader never learns how the two kinds of slabs compared.

D.why: You stretched the conclusion beyond the notes. The team said basalt bars 'could help' decks last longer. Claiming that every deck in a cold climate will last twice as long goes well past what 24 test slabs can show.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the aim of Banerjee and Duggan's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Many US states now bar employers from asking job applicants how much they earned in previous jobs.
• Economists Rhea Banerjee and Colm Duggan investigated whether workers who change jobs get bigger raises in states with these bans than in states without them.
• They compared pay records for 40,000 job changers in ban states and in neighboring states with no ban.
• Pay rose an average of 9% after a job change in ban states and 5% in states without bans.
• The economists concluded that the bans strengthen workers' bargaining position.
choices: Banerjee and Duggan wanted to know whether workers who switch jobs get larger raises in states that ban salary-history questions than in states that don't.
Banerjee and Duggan found that job changers' pay rose by an average of 9% in states with salary-history bans but by only 5% in states without them.
Banerjee and Duggan concluded that banning salary-history questions gives job applicants a stronger position when they negotiate pay with employers.
Banerjee and Duggan examined the pay records of 40,000 workers who changed jobs, some in ban states and some in neighboring states without a ban.
explanation: 'Aim' means the question the study set out to answer. Choice A is built around 'wanted to know whether', and it says exactly what the economists were trying to learn: whether job changers in ban states get bigger raises than those in states without bans.

B.why: You reported the result rather than the aim. The 9% versus 5% gap is what the study found, not what it set out to investigate.

C.why: You picked the conclusion, the last stage of the study. It tells your reader what the economists decided after the study, not what question they began with.

D.why: You picked the method. Saying whose records were examined describes how the study worked, but it never states the question the study was meant to answer.

stem: The student wants to present the study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Some urban planners argue that planting trees along a street makes drivers slow down.
• Planner Inês Carvalho tested this claim on residential streets in Porto, Portugal.
• She measured traffic speeds on 30 tree-lined streets and on 30 similar streets without trees.
• Drivers averaged 38 km/h on the tree-lined streets and 46 km/h on the streets without trees.
• Carvalho concluded that street trees could be a low-cost way to calm traffic.
choices: Some urban planners argue that the trees planted along a residential street can lead drivers to slow down, an idea Inês Carvalho decided to test in Porto.
Measuring speeds on 30 tree-lined and 30 treeless streets in Porto, Carvalho found that drivers averaged 8 km/h slower on the streets with trees.
Measuring speeds on 30 tree-lined and 30 treeless streets in Porto, Carvalho found that drivers averaged 8 km/h faster on the streets with trees.
After her work in Porto, Inês Carvalho concluded that planting trees along streets could be an inexpensive way for cities to calm traffic.
explanation: 'The study and its findings' needs two things: what the study did and what it found. Choice B names the study (speeds measured on 30 tree-lined and 30 treeless streets in Porto) and gives the finding as a gap: drivers averaged 8 km/h slower where there were trees (38 versus 46 km/h).

A.why: You picked the background. It sets up the debate and mentions that Carvalho tested it, but it never says what she found, so half of the goal is missing.

C.why: You got the direction of the gap backward. Drivers were slower on tree-lined streets (38 km/h) than on treeless ones (46 km/h), not faster. When the goal turns on a difference, check which way it runs.

D.why: You picked the conclusion alone. It gives Carvalho's interpretation but neither the street measurements nor the speeds, so it presents neither the study nor its findings.
